messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 51
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Tax Inspector
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 39

He is 51, a South Eastern Asian man who has spent most of his adult life trying to be reliable, measured, and hard to rattle. He works as a tax inspector, a role that suits the careful, orderly way he likes to move through the world. Before the events that bring him to therapy, he describes himself as private but steady, someone his wife could count on to handle practical problems and keep the household on track.

The trauma begins in a relationship he once experiences as loving and familiar. Over time, his romantic partner becomes increasingly controlling, then physically abusive. At first, he minimizes the shoving, the grabbing of his arms, the slap that leaves him stunned more than injured. He tells himself the violence is a bad moment, an argument gone too far, and that if he stays calm the situation will settle. Instead, the episodes escalate. He starts to live with a quiet vigilance, monitoring footsteps, tone of voice, the sound of doors closing. He learns to read anger before it fully appears. There is a particular terror in how ordinary the days look from the outside; he continues going to work, continues paying bills, continues speaking in a composed voice while his body stays braced for the next blow.

After one especially violent incident, he realizes he is not merely frightened but trapped in a pattern of humiliation and threat. Even then, leaving does not happen cleanly. He feels ashamed of what has been happening, especially because as a man he believes he should have been able to stop it. He says very little to others. He protects the relationship’s image and his own dignity by keeping the abuse secret, and that secrecy becomes part of the injury. He starts sleeping lightly, waking to small sounds, checking locks more than once. At home he finds himself standing with his back to a wall, unconsciously choosing the room positions that feel safest. He notices that his chest tightens when someone raises a hand quickly, even in harmless gestures. At work, where precision matters, he remains competent but increasingly tense. He rereads forms, double-checks figures, and has to fight off moments when his mind drifts back to the most recent assault. He feels embarrassed by how easily his concentration breaks, as if the part of him that once handled complex tasks with ease is now always partly elsewhere.

In the months after the abuse stops, he expects relief and instead finds that his body keeps the memory alive. He is startled by sharp voices, by the sound of someone arguing in a neighboring apartment, by the thud of a dropped object. When this happens, he goes still and feels his heart race before he can think. He avoids crowded places when he can, preferring predictable routines and familiar routes. He becomes uncomfortable when strangers stand too close. Certain moments catch him off guard: the smell of alcohol, a particular kind of angry silence, the sight of a clenched jaw. He does not talk about these reactions much, but he notices how they shape his days. He is irritable with small disruptions, then feels guilty for snapping at his wife or withdrawing when she asks if he is all right.

He also carries a persistent inner burden of self-blame. He returns again and again to questions of why he did not leave sooner, why he stayed so long, why he did not protect himself better. At night he thinks about the relationship in fragments, not as a coherent story but as flashes of fear and shame. Sleep does not feel restorative; he wakes tired and already tense, as though he has been working through the night. He finds little pleasure in the things that used to settle him, including quiet meals and weekend errands with his wife. Instead, he often feels numb, cut off from the ease and warmth that used to come more naturally.

Still, he continues to function in the outward ways that have always mattered to him. He goes to work, keeps appointments, answers questions carefully, and presents as composed. But those who know him best can see that he moves through the world with more caution now. He is slower to trust his own sense of safety, and when he is alone, he often sits in silence, listening to the house and waiting for his body to relax, which it rarely does fully.
